newsitem.title: USA: Stocks and bonds tumble as inflation worries revive.
newsitem.headline: Stocks and bonds tumble as inflation worries revive.

text.p: The stock and bond markets took a beating on Friday as fresh worries about inflation sent investors running for cover.
The dollar posted its biggest one-day loss in three months, while gold prices rallied as investors sought a safe haven against inflation.
Stocks tumbled as investors sold off under the mounting pressure of rapidly surging interest rates in the bond market.
The Dow Jones industrial average slid 156.78 points, or nearly 2 percent, to end at 8,031.22. It was the ninth-largest decline ever for the blue-chip average.
In the broader market, decliners beat advancers 2,456 to 526 on heavy volume of 561.3 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange. Weekly volume totalled 2.69 billion shares.

As on Thursday, when the Dow fell 71.31 points, stocks were hurt on Friday by weakness in the bond market, where the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury slid 1-14/32, or $14.38 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.64 percent from 6.53 percent on Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Worries that retail sales data for July would come in surprisingly strong and prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates swept through the bond market Friday. Although the retail sales figures aren't due out until next Wednesday, the jitters were enough to touch off a wave of heavy selling.

"The two props to valuation levels in this market have been interest rates, which have been trending lower, and earnings, which have been surprisingly good," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management.
"This month, at least so far, we have had the bond market reversing course and nothing sufficiently positive to hold the market up," he said.
The rapid turnaround in interest rates has come amid a sudden flurry of signs that economic growth may have started to accelerate after a tame second quarter.
The evidence, found first in manufacturing and employment reports last week, has sent the long-bond yield up from an 18-month low of 6.31 percent a little more than a week ago.
"The markets have done so well lately," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney. "It doesn't take much to trigger profit-taking."
With little in the way of earnings news to act on, analysts said markets in the coming days would resume their obsessive search for any sign of accelerating inflation.
In addition to retail sales, wholesale and consumer price reports are due next week.

The dollar, battered by heavy selling of stocks and bonds and a sharp downturn in the British pound against European currencies and the Japanese yen, posted its biggest one-day losses in three months on Friday.

The dollar fell to 1.8452 marks from 1.8690 marks late on Thursday, its biggest one-day drop since May 20. The dollar settled at 114.80 yen, down from 118.43 yen late on Thursday, its biggest one-day loss since May 9.

Gold prices, benefitting from the sharp slide in stocks, bonds and the dollar, surged to their highest level in a week. Gold for December delivery rose $4.60 to $330.40 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange after hitting a one-week peak of $332 during the session.

Overseas, Britain's FTSE 100 closed at 5,031.3, down 55.5 points on the day but up 132 points on the week. Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average closed at 19,604.46, up 128.61 points but down 199.92 on the week.
